messages.speaker: Dev
messages.text: Made the mushroom risotto tonight and it came out gluey. What did I do wrong?

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: Did you rinse the rice first? Washing arborio strips the starch you actually want.

messages.speaker: Dev
messages.text: I did rinse it. Also I dumped all the stock in at once because I was in a hurry.

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: There it is. Add the stock a ladle at a time and stir. That is what releases starch slowly and gives you creaminess without glue.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: Also take it off the heat while the grains still have a little bite. It keeps cooking in the pan.

messages.speaker: Dev
messages.text: How much stock for 300g of rice?

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: Roughly a litre, but go by texture rather than the number. Some days the rice drinks more.

messages.speaker: Dev
messages.text: Second attempt was much better. Still not restaurant level but I would serve it.

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: That is the right bar. Restaurant level uses about twice the butter you think is reasonable.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: And a stock that has been going for six hours.

messages.speaker: Dev
messages.text: So it is not me, it is the fat and the time.

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: Mostly, yes.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: My bread keeps coming out dense. Crumb is tight and it barely rises.

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: How warm is your kitchen? Dough proves painfully slowly under about 20 degrees.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: Maybe 17 at the moment, the heating has been off.

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: Then give it longer, not more yeast. Two hours at 17 degrees is nowhere near two hours at 24.

messages.speaker: Dev
messages.text: The oven with just the light on is a decent proving box, about 26 degrees.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: That is a good trick, I will try it tomorrow.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: Proved it in the oven with the light on and it doubled in ninety minutes instead of not at all.

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: There you go. Nothing was wrong with your recipe, only the room.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: How do I know when it is properly proved rather than just bigger?

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: Press it with a floured finger. If the dent springs back slowly and only part way, it is ready.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: And if it springs back immediately?

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: Needs longer. If it does not spring back at all you have gone too far.

messages.speaker: Dev
messages.text: What happens if you overprove it?

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: It collapses in the oven and you get a flat loaf with a dense streak near the base.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: That is exactly what happened to me in January.

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: Then you now know both failure modes, which is most of the way there.

messages.speaker: Priya
messages.text: Can someone settle an argument. Do you salt pasta water before or after it boils?

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: It makes no real difference to the pasta. Salting after it boils just avoids pitting the bottom of the pan.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: The amount matters far more than the timing. It should taste properly seasoned, not faintly salty.

messages.speaker: Priya
messages.text: How much is properly seasoned in grams?

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: About 10g per litre of water. Any less and the pasta is bland no matter what sauce you put on it.

messages.speaker: Priya
messages.text: That is much more than I have been using.

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: It usually is. Most people use about a third of what they should.

messages.speaker: Dev
messages.text: Does the pasta actually absorb it, or does it just wash off?

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: It absorbs it while it cooks. That is why seasoning the sauce harder does not fix bland pasta.

messages.speaker: Priya
messages.text: Tried it properly salted and the difference is embarrassing.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: It is the single cheapest improvement in cooking.

messages.speaker: Priya
messages.text: What about oil in the water?

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: Pointless. It floats on top and the only thing it does is stop sauce clinging later.

messages.speaker: Priya
messages.text: I have been doing that for years.

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: Most of us were taught it. It is just wrong.

messages.speaker: Dev
messages.text: What are we all cooking for the meetup on Saturday?

messages.speaker: Priya
messages.text: I will bring a dal, it travels well and reheats without going strange.

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: I will do a tray of roasted vegetables and a big salad. Two people coming are vegetarian.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: Then I will handle bread and something sweet. Sourdough if the proving goes better this time.

messages.speaker: Dev
messages.text: I can bring the risotto if I have redeemed myself by then.

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: Risotto does not survive a car journey. Bring something that likes sitting around instead.

messages.speaker: Dev
messages.text: Fair. A slow cooked ragu then, that only improves overnight.

messages.speaker: Priya
messages.text: Does anyone have a nut allergy coming? I want to know before I put cashews in anything.

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: One of Sam's friends cannot have peanuts. Tree nuts are fine but label the dish anyway.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: Confirmed, peanuts only. I will bring cards so every dish says what is in it.

messages.speaker: Priya
messages.text: Perfect. What time are we starting?

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: Doors at six, eating around seven. Come earlier if you need oven space.

messages.speaker: Dev
messages.text: I will need the oven for twenty minutes to reheat, so I will get there at half five.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: I need it hot for the bread, so I will come at five and go first.

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: Then the order is Sam at five, Dev at half five, everything else is cold or stovetop.

messages.speaker: Priya
messages.text: Should someone bring plates? Eleven is a lot for one kitchen.

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: I have eight. If two people bring three each we are fine.

messages.speaker: Dev
messages.text: I will bring plates and cutlery.

messages.speaker: Priya
messages.text: And I will bring glasses.

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: That went well. Nothing was cold and nobody had to eat standing up.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: The bread was the best I have made. Twelve hour cold prove in the fridge.

messages.speaker: Dev
messages.text: That is what made the difference?

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: I think so. The flavour was completely different, much more sour and complex.

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: Cold proving does that. The yeast slows down but the bacteria keep working.

messages.speaker: Priya
messages.text: Is that the same thing as sourdough?

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: Related. Sourdough uses wild yeast and bacteria together from the start. Cold proving a normal dough gets you partway there.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: Much less commitment too. No starter to feed.

messages.speaker: Dev
messages.text: How much work is a starter really?

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: Once it is established, five minutes every few days if you keep it in the fridge.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: It is the establishing that is the work. Two weeks of feeding before it does anything useful.

messages.speaker: Dev
messages.text: Would you do it again from scratch?

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: Yes, but I would not pretend it is low effort.

messages.speaker: Priya
messages.text: My dal was too thin on Saturday. How do I fix that next time?

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: Less water at the start is easier than reducing at the end.

messages.speaker: Priya
messages.text: How much less?

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: Start at three parts water to one part lentils and add more if it needs it. You cannot take water out.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: You can also blend a ladleful and stir it back in. Thickens it without changing the flavour.

messages.speaker: Priya
messages.text: That is a good trick.

messages.speaker: Dev
messages.text: Does the type of lentil change it?

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: Very much. Red lentils collapse into a puree, brown and green hold their shape.

messages.speaker: Priya
messages.text: I used red, and it did go quite soft.

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: Then it was doing what it was meant to. It just needed less liquid.

messages.speaker: Dev
messages.text: Stupid question. Why do my onions never go properly brown?

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: How long are you giving them?

messages.speaker: Dev
messages.text: Ten minutes maybe.

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: There is your answer. Properly caramelised onions take forty five minutes at least.

messages.speaker: Dev
messages.text: Forty five? Every recipe says ten.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: Every recipe is lying. Ten minutes gets you soft and translucent, not brown and sweet.

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: Add a pinch of salt early to draw water out and it goes a little faster, but not much.

messages.speaker: Dev
messages.text: Can I rush it with higher heat?

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: No. Higher heat burns the outside before the sugars develop. Low and slow is the whole trick.

messages.speaker: Dev
messages.text: Forty minutes later and they are basically jam. This is a completely different ingredient.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: Now you know why French onion soup takes all afternoon.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: What is everyone doing for the next meetup? Same format or something different?

messages.speaker: Priya
messages.text: Could we each cook one thing from the same country?

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: I like that. It stops us all bringing roasted vegetables.

messages.speaker: Dev
messages.text: Which country?

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: Somewhere none of us cook from often. Georgia? Vietnam?

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: Vietnam. Lots of it travels well and half of it is meant to be eaten at room temperature.

messages.speaker: Priya
messages.text: I am in. I will do the herb salad and the dipping sauce.

messages.speaker: Dev
messages.text: I will attempt the caramelised pork. It is the one I keep meaning to try.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: Then I will do banh mi, which means I get to make bread again.

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: Predictable and welcome. I will do the soup.

messages.speaker: Priya
messages.text: Do we need a rice cooker? I do not own one.

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: I have one and I will bring it. It saves a hob.

messages.speaker: Dev
messages.text: How many are we this time?

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: Nine confirmed so far.

messages.speaker: Priya
messages.text: Same allergy situation?

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: Peanuts again, and this cuisine uses them constantly, so we need to be careful.

messages.speaker: Nora
messages.text: Then label everything and keep one peanut free version of the sauce separate.

messages.speaker: Priya
messages.text: I will make two batches and keep them apart from the start.

messages.speaker: Sam
messages.text: That is the safest way. Cross contamination is the real risk, not the ingredient list.
